hints: Look at the carbon in carvone bonded to the isopropyl group and check how many different groups are attached to it.
walkthrough:
Spot the possible stereocentre**
Look closely at the ring carbon carrying the $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$ type side chain, actually $\text{C}(\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2)(\text{CH}_3)$. It is $sp^3$ and bonded to H, to the isopropylalkene group, and to two different directions round the ring (one side toward C=O, one side toward C=C). Those four groups are all different, so that carbon is chiral.
Final answer: Optical isomerism, as carvone contains a chiral carbon atom bonded to four different groups.

hints: Count the H atoms added by comparing carvone with X: two C=C bonds are saturated and one C=O becomes CH-OH.
First write the two molecular formulae $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$ and $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{20}\text{O}$, then balance H with $\text{H}_2$.
walkthrough:
Work out what hydrogen does**
In carvone you have two $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bonds (one in the ring, one in the side chain) and one $\text{C}=\text{O}$ ketone. In X you have no $\text{C}=\text{C}$ and the ketone has become a secondary alcohol $\text{CH-OH}$. Each $\text{C}=\text{C}$ needs one $\text{H}_2$ and $\text{C}=\text{O}$ to $\text{CH-OH}$ needs one $\text{H}_2$.

Write formulae then balance**
Carvone is $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$ and X is $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{20}\text{O}$. The H difference is $6$ H atoms, so $3\text{H}_2$ is needed: $$\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}\text{O} + 3\text{H}_2 \longrightarrow \text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{20}\text{O}$$

hints: Recall the characteristic mechanism by which an alkyl group replaces H on a benzene ring using a halogenoalkane and $\text{AlCl}_3$.
walkthrough:
Recognise the benzene pattern**
Step 1 puts an isopropyl group onto methylbenzene to give 1-methyl-4-(propan-2-yl)benzene. Whenever H on a benzene ring is replaced by an electrophile and the aromatic ring is regenerated, think electrophilic substitution. Here it is the Friedel-Crafts alkylation version.

hints: In step 3 $\text{NO}_2$ becomes $\text{NH}_2$ with gain of H and loss of O, decide if this is oxidation or reduction.
In step 5 the $\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$ group is replaced by $\text{OH}$, decide what general class this replacement belongs to.
walkthrough:
Classify step 3**
$\text{Ar-NO}_2$ to $\text{Ar-NH}_2$ gains hydrogen and loses oxygen. That is gain of electrons, so it is reduction of the nitro group.

Classify step 5**
$\text{Ar-N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$ to $\text{Ar-OH}$ replaces the diazonium group by $\text{OH}$ on warming with water. That is substitution, often called hydrolysis of the diazonium salt.

Final answer: step 3: reduction
step 5: substitution / hydrolysis

hints: For step 1 to add $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$, think which chloroalkane plus which Lewis acid catalyst generates that carbocation.
For step 2 to add $\text{NO}_2$ ortho to methyl, recall the standard nitrating mixture for benzene.
For step 3 to convert $\text{NO}_2$ to $\text{NH}_2$, recall the metal plus concentrated acid reducing agent used for aromatic nitro compounds.
For step 4 to convert $\text{NH}_2$ to $\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$, recall the nitrous acid reagent made in situ.
Remember nitration of an activated ring must be kept cool to avoid multiple nitration.
Remember diazotisation is unstable above $10^{\circ}\text{C}$ and must be kept in ice.
walkthrough:
Build step 1, Friedel-Crafts alkylation**
You need to attach $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$. Use 2-chloropropane, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCl}$, with anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ catalyst ( $\text{FeCl}_3$ works similarly). The catalyst generates the $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}^+$ electrophile which attacks the ring para to methyl.

Build step 2, nitration**
Nitration always uses concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ plus concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ which makes the $\text{NO}_2^+$ electrophile. Because the ring has two activating alkyl groups, keep $T < 55^{\circ}\text{C}$ to get mononitration ortho to the methyl group as shown.

Build step 3, nitro reduction**
Convert $\text{Ar-NO}_2$ to $\text{Ar-NH}_2$ with $\text{Sn}$ and concentrated $\text{HCl}$ under heat, followed by alkali to free the amine. This is the classic A Level reducing system for aromatic nitro groups.

Build step 4, diazotisation**
Convert $\text{Ar-NH}_2$ to $\text{Ar-N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$ with nitrous acid, $\text{HNO}_2$, made in situ from $\text{NaNO}_2 + \text{HCl}$. Keep $T < 10^{\circ}\text{C}$ (ice bath) or the diazonium salt decomposes and gives phenol prematurely.

Final answer: step 1: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCl}$ with $\text{AlCl}_3$ (or $\text{AlBr}_3$ / $\text{FeCl}_3$ / $\text{FeBr}_3$)
step 2: conc. $\text{HNO}_3$ + conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, $T < 55^{\circ}\text{C}$
step 3: $\text{Sn}$ + conc. $\text{HCl}$ (heat, then $\text{NaOH}$ to liberate amine)
step 4: $\text{NaNO}_2$ + $\text{HCl}$ (i.e. $\text{HNO}_2$) , $T < 10^{\circ}\text{C}$

hints: Recall what reagent hydrogenates a benzene ring to a cyclohexane ring and why forcing conditions are needed to destroy aromatic stability.
walkthrough:
Force hydrogen onto an aromatic ring**
A benzene ring is very stable, so ordinary $\text{H}_2$/Ni at room conditions will not touch it. You need $\text{H}_2$ with a nickel (or platinum) catalyst under high temperature and high pressure to add three molecules of $\text{H}_2$ across the three double bonds and give the cyclohexane ring.
Final answer: $\text{H}_2$ with Ni catalyst (or Pt) with heat and high pressure.

hints: Place $\text{CH}_3$ at the top carbon, $\text{OH}$ on the next carbon clockwise, and $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$ at the bottom para carbon as in X.
Since all six H atoms add from the same face of the flat benzene, all three alkyl and OH groups must end up on the opposite face, so draw them all wedged (or all dashed).
walkthrough:
Put the groups in the right places**
Copy the skeleton of X: methyl at the top, OH ortho to it, and isopropyl $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$ para to methyl at the bottom of the cyclohexane. That satisfies the connectivity mark.

Make the addition cis**
Picture the flat benzene with $\text{H}_2$ approaching only from below. All new $\text{C-H}$ bonds form below the ring, so the existing $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{OH}$ and isopropyl groups are all pushed above the ring together. Show this by drawing all three substituent bonds as solid wedges (or all as hashed wedges). That gives the all cis isomer where all H atoms are on the same side.

Final answer: Structure of X with $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}$, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{OH}$ on the correct ring positions, with all three substituents cis to each other (all wedges, or all dashes), meaning all ring H atoms are on the same opposite side.
